lines: A single immutable file, Parquet or ORC, still can't answer what a table actually means once the storage underneath isn't a file system at all.
This topic opens exactly that substrate: what object storage really guarantees today, and the one primitive every later topic in this chapter leans on.
Here's a simple question. Write an object to S three, and the instant that write succeeds, read it back.
Does that read see the new object right away, or could it still see stale data for a little while?
answer: It always sees the new object immediately. S three has delivered strong read-after-write consistency for every request since December of twenty twenty.
Before that change, it was only eventually consistent — a read right after a write really could come back stale.

lines: Before December of twenty twenty, S three was eventually consistent. A read right after a write might still return the old version, or nothing at all.
Since that change, any read that comes after a successful write response sees the new object immediately, every single time, with no window where it could still be stale.
Here's something object storage genuinely does not give you: an atomic rename. What people call a rename is really two separate requests — copy the object under a new name, then delete the old one.
Run that against a real local object-storage server and stop right after the copy, before the delete. Both the original and the copy exist at the same time.
Nothing in the protocol stops that. A crash between the two calls is a real, reachable state, not a hypothetical one.
steps.takeaway: A rename that's really copy-then-delete has no atomicity between the two calls — a crash in between leaves both objects sitting there.

lines: Now picture two writers racing for the same key at almost the same instant, with no external lock service coordinating them.
Can they both succeed?
answer: No. A conditional header makes the object store itself pick exactly one winner — the other request gets rejected outright.
Without that header, the last write to land on disk just silently overwrites whatever was there before.

lines: Watch this happen for real. Writer A sends a create with the If-None-Match header set to the wildcard, meaning only succeed if this key doesn't exist yet. It succeeds.
Writer B sends the exact same kind of request for the exact same key, against the same real server. It comes back rejected, with a genuine Precondition Failed error — not a simulated one.
If-None-Match handles creation. If-Match is the same idea for updates — a real compare-and-swap on the object's current ETag.

Send an update carrying the object's current ETag, and it commits. Send that same update again, but now the ETag you're holding is stale because someone else already changed it — rejected, the exact same way.
steps.takeaway: If-Match turns an update into a real compare-and-swap — a stale ETag gets rejected exactly like a conflicting create.

lines: One more thing object storage doesn't give you for free: listing. A real paginated listing of two hundred fifty objects, fifty objects per page, takes five separate round trips, not one.
And every prefix has its own request-rate ceiling. Push past it and the object store starts throttling you, prefix by prefix.
Put it together, and here's what that one conditional-write primitive actually buys you.
Without it, two writers racing for the same key end with whichever write happened to land last — silently, with no error, no signal that anything was lost.
With If-None-Match or If-Match in place, exactly one writer's commit survives, and the object store itself enforces that, with no external coordination service at all.
steps.takeaway: Conditional writes are an atomic compare-and-swap built right into object storage — no external lock service required.

lines: Step back, and here's the shape of it. Reads have been strongly consistent since twenty twenty, so that worry is gone for good.
Rename never was atomic, and it still isn't — that one hasn't changed.
What has changed is the commit primitive. If-None-Match and If-Match turn object storage from a place you merely store bytes into a place you can actually commit to, one writer at a time.
